learn.hook: A recipe for chai, the steps for long division and the instructions inside your phone's map app have something in common: they are all algorithms!
points: An algorithm is a finite list of clear, step-by-step instructions that solves a problem or completes a task.
A good algorithm has an input (what you start with), an output (the result), and steps that are precise, so anyone following them gets the same result.
It must stop after a finite number of steps.
The order of steps matters: 'add 3, then double' is not the same as 'double, then add 3'.
Algorithms can repeat steps (loops) and make choices (if this, then do that).

example.q: Algorithm: start with a number. If it is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Stop when you reach 1. Start with 6. How many steps until you reach 1?

learn.reallife: Railway ticket booking, ATM cash withdrawal and traffic signals all run on algorithms written by programmers.

games.title: Algorithm for making chai
items: Boil a cup of water in a pan
Add tea leaves and let it boil for a minute
Add milk and sugar and boil again
Strain the chai into a cup

games.title: Clear step or vague step?
items: Do something nice with the number
Keep going until it feels right

quiz.q: Which is the best description of an algorithm?
options: A finite list of clear steps that solves a problem
Any computer program, even one that never stops
A list of answers to memorise
quiz.explain: An algorithm must be step-by-step, precise and finite.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only computer code can be an algorithm

quiz.q: Which instruction would be a poor step in an algorithm?
options: Stop when the total is above 100
quiz.explain: 'A little' and 'maybe' are vague; two people could follow this step differently.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that a step must be precise

quiz.q: Start with 5. Repeat 3 times: double the number and then add 1. What is the result?
quiz.mistake: Stops after two repeats (23) or does one repeat too many (95)

quiz.q: In an algorithm for making chai, what are the inputs?
options: Water, tea leaves, milk and sugar
quiz.explain: Inputs are what the algorithm starts with. The cup of chai is the output.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the input with the output

quiz.q: Use the rule: if even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; stop at 1. Starting from 12, how many steps until you reach 1?
quiz.mistake: Counts the numbers in the chain (10) instead of the steps between them

quiz.q: Why must an algorithm have a finite number of steps?
options: So that it fits on one page
So that it eventually stops and gives an answer
Because computers can only count to 100
quiz.explain: A procedure that never stops can never give an output.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the length limit is about writing space

quiz.q: Algorithm A: add 3, then multiply by 2. Algorithm B: multiply by 2, then add 3. Both start with 5. What is A's result minus B's result?
quiz.explain: A gives (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. B gives 5 × 2 + 3 = 13. 16 − 13 = 3, so order matters.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the order of steps does not change the result

quiz.q: To find the largest number in a list, keep a 'biggest so far' and replace it only when a number is BIGGER. For the list 7, 3, 12, 9, 12, 5, how many times is 'biggest so far' replaced after starting with 7?
quiz.explain: Only the first 12 is bigger than 7. The second 12 is equal, not bigger, so no change.
quiz.mistake: Replaces the value when a number is equal, counting 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "My mum's recipe says 'cook till done'. Is that an algorithm?"
teach.praise: An algorithm needs clear, precise steps in the right order that finish with an answer. 'Till done' is too vague for a computer!
teach.nudge: Would two different people understand 'cook till done' in exactly the same way? What makes a step good?

learn.hook: Over 2000 years ago Euclid found a way to get the HCF of two huge numbers without listing a single factor. It is still used in every computer today!
points: Division algorithm: for whole numbers a and b > 0, a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b.

Euclid's algorithm for HCF(a, b): divide the larger by the smaller, then replace the pair by (smaller, remainder). Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder (the last divisor) is the HCF.
LCM(a, b) = a × b ÷ HCF(a, b).
To test if n is prime, you only need to try dividing by primes up to √n.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to a limit by crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7, ... Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by halving the search area each time.

example.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(252, 105).
steps: The remainder is 0, so the HCF is the last divisor, 21

learn.reallife: Online payments are kept safe by codes that use Euclid's algorithm and prime numbers. Searching a contact on your phone uses ideas like binary search.

quiz.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(48, 18).
quiz.mistake: Stops early and gives the first remainder (12)

quiz.q: Find HCF(91, 65) using Euclid's algorithm.
quiz.mistake: Gives a remainder from the middle of the process instead of the last divisor

quiz.q: To check whether 97 is prime, what is the largest prime you need to try dividing by?
quiz.explain: √97 is a little less than 10, so you only need to try 2, 3, 5 and 7. None divides 97, so 97 is prime.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must try every number up to half of 97

quiz.q: Riya thinks of a number from 1 to 100. Arjun always guesses the middle of the remaining range and is told 'higher' or 'lower'. What is the most guesses he will ever need?
quiz.explain: After each wrong guess at most half of the numbers are left: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12 → 6 → 3 → 1. After 6 guesses only one number can remain, so the 7th guess is sure to be right (2⁷ = 128 ≥ 100).
quiz.mistake: Thinks you might need to try every number one by one

quiz.q: HCF(12, 18) = 6. What is LCM(12, 18)?
quiz.mistake: Gives the product 216 without dividing by the HCF

quiz.q: After using the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the numbers 1 to 100, how many primes are left?
quiz.explain: Crossing out 1 and the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not those primes themselves) leaves exactly 25 primes up to 100.
quiz.mistake: Thinks half the numbers (all the odd ones) are prime

quiz.q: Use repeated subtraction (the older form of Euclid's method) for HCF(35, 14): keep subtracting the smaller from the larger. What is the HCF?
quiz.explain: (35, 14) → (21, 14) → (7, 14) → (7, 7). When the two numbers are equal, that number, 7, is the HCF.
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first subtraction

quiz.q: Write 157 = 12 × q + r with 0 ≤ r < 12. What is r?
quiz.explain: 12 × 13 = 156, so 157 = 12 × 13 + 1. The remainder is 1.
quiz.mistake: Gives the quotient (13) instead of the remainder

teach.ask: Gappu wants the HCF of 1071 and 462: "Listing all their factors will take forever! Is there a faster way?"
teach.praise: Euclid's algorithm: divide, take the remainder, and repeat with the smaller numbers until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the HCF. It is 21!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the remainder after the first division? When do you stop?

learn.hook: Before a robot vacuum cleans your room, someone had to think like a computer: break the job into tiny steps, repeat them and make decisions. That is algorithmic thinking!
points: Decomposition: break a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
Loops repeat a set of steps, either a fixed number of times or while a condition is true.
Conditions (if... else...) let an algorithm choose between different steps.
Flowcharts show algorithms as pictures: ovals for start and stop, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions (yes/no questions), and arrows for the order.
Efficiency: different algorithms can solve the same problem in very different numbers of steps. Tracing an algorithm step by step helps you find and fix bugs.

example.q: Trace this algorithm: set x = 1. While x is less than 50, replace x by 3 × x. Output x.
steps: 81 is not less than 50, so stop and output 81

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' route planning, Diwali light patterns on a timer and video games all use loops and conditions.

items.text: Breaking a big task into smaller tasks is called ___
A set of steps that repeats is called a ___
A mistake in an algorithm is often called a ___
'If marks ≥ 33, print Pass, else print Fail' is an example of a ___

quiz.q: In a flowchart, what does a diamond-shaped box show?
quiz.explain: A diamond holds a question, and the flow splits into 'yes' and 'no' paths.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the decision box with the action box

quiz.q: A total starts at 10. A loop runs 5 times, and each time it adds 4 to the total. What is the final total?
quiz.explain: 5 additions of 4 add 20, so the total becomes 10 + 20 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the starting value of 10

quiz.q: Set x = 2. While x is less than 100, replace x by x × x. What is the output?
quiz.explain: 2 → 4 → 16 → 256. 16 is still less than 100, so the loop runs once more, giving 256.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 16, forgetting to check the condition one more time

quiz.q: Which algorithm finds 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 1000 in the fewest steps?
options: Add the numbers one by one
quiz.explain: The formula needs just a multiplication and a division: 1000 × 1001 ÷ 2 = 500500, instead of 999 additions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every correct method is equally efficient

quiz.q: An algorithm says: 'If marks are 33 or more, print Pass; else print Fail.' Meena scores exactly 33. What is printed?
quiz.explain: 33 or more includes 33 itself, so the condition is true and Pass is printed.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'or more' as 'more than'

quiz.q: Harpreet's algorithm for the average of three numbers says: 'Add them, then divide by 2.' What is the correct average of 6, 9 and 12?
quiz.explain: The bug is dividing by 2. The correct average is (6 + 9 + 12) ÷ 3 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
steps: Divide by 3, the number of values
quiz.mistake: Follows the buggy step and gets 13.5

quiz.q: What is it called when you break a big problem, like planning a school trip, into smaller tasks?
quiz.explain: Decomposition means splitting a problem into parts: booking a bus, collecting money, planning food, and so on.
quiz.mistake: Confuses decomposition with repetition (looping)

quiz.q: For each of 4 rows, Kabir's algorithm says 'place 6 diyas'. How many times is a diya placed in total?
quiz.explain: The inner step runs 6 times for each of the 4 rows: 4 × 6 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the loop counts instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu wants to teach a robot to water 10 plants: "Do I really have to write 'water the plant' ten times?"
teach.praise: Use a loop: repeat 'water the plant and move on' 10 times, or until no plants are left. Smart robot, smarter bird!
teach.nudge: Is there a way to tell the robot to do the same step again and again? How will it know when to stop?
